samples.hyp: The necessity of conducting mass screening for SARS-CoV-2 to prevent a potential outbreak in the Lusaka district, the capital city of Zambia, by including asymptomatic individuals in the testing.
Simple mathematical modeling study

In Africa, the novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19) caused by the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is thought to be primarily spread by individuals who are asymptomatic (or have mild symptoms) for the infection.
It is still not definitively known to what extent asymptomatic individuals contribute to the transmission of infection.
However, studies indicate that their management situation is very crucial for controlling the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

In Zambia's Lusaka district, to control the outbreak, a simple mathematical model named "exposed-infected-recovered" (EIR) was developed to assess the impact of asymptomatic individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 on the overall transmission dynamics.
For this, we modeled two scenarios: (1) asymptomatic individuals account for about 70% of all COVID-19 cases, and (2) asymptomatic individuals account for only about 50% of the cases.

In summary, the model initially assumes that asymptomatic individuals transmit infections equally as symptomatic individuals. However, in a secondary and more likely scenario, asymptomatic individuals are estimated to transmit infections at about half the rate of symptomatic individuals.

A model that assumes 70% of cases are asymptomatic suggests that a minimum and high daily testing rate of ≥ 7911 tests/100,000 population is sufficient to control the outbreak if about half of the asymptomatic individuals are infectious. If equal infectiousness is assumed, a testing rate of ≥ 10028 tests/100,000 population is necessary.

For 50% of individuals without symptoms, a comprehensive testing rate of ≥ 4540 tests per 100,000 population is sufficient to control the outbreak at the expected level of infection transmission when compared to individuals with symptoms.
Discussion and Conclusion

Our model suggests that mass testing, including asymptomatic individuals, can be used to monitor the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, to control COVID-19 outbreaks; however, this approach is very costly.
Large-scale wastewater testing in major cities like Lusaka can potentially curb the spread of COVID-19; however, is this feasible?
In 2020, as computer models predicted, by extensively testing people and isolating those who test positive, it is possible to control the spread of COVID-19 in large cities.
However, researchers have stated that this approach may be expensive and impractical.
At the beginning of the pandemic, many people infected with COVID-19 were transmitting the disease to others without showing any symptoms.

Some studies have indicated that between 50% to 80% of individuals with COVID-19 were asymptomatic (showed no symptoms of the disease), and similarly, they could be responsible for 40% to 70% of new infections.
Researchers wanted to know if identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals could help reduce the spread of COVID-19.
Additionally, mass screenings, meaning examining many people at once, effectively identify asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers have developed a predictive computer model that simulates how individuals transition from being exposed to infection, to becoming infected, and then to recovery.
They focused on information obtained from the Lusaka region of Zambia, which has its own international airport, shares borders with two countries, and is a corporate hub.

Four mutations of COVID-19 were identified as appearing to vary from place to place, and these mutations were found in 50% to 70% of COVID-19 cases that were asymptomatic, and these mutations were equally or half as infectious as those with symptoms.

According to the researchers' model, controlling the spread of COVID-19 can be achieved by conducting comprehensive investigations and isolating individuals who test positive, as well as those without symptoms.
In all mutations, about 10% of asymptomatic individuals had to be monitored daily to reduce the high mutation rate by 90%.
Additionally, if we want to stop the rise of new COVID-19 infections, about 22% of people need to be tested daily.
Zambia seems to be extending many measures to combat COVID-19, yet the cases appear to be increasing.
In a small town in Italy, mass testing has reduced COVID-19 cases by 90% in a controlled manner.
However, there are no previous studies indicating that it could be equally effective in another large city.

The researchers who should have been cautious did not conduct mass surveys in this study; instead, they developed a model suggesting that mass testing in large cities could curb the spread of COVID-19.
However, it is thought that it could be very expensive.
In addition to movement restrictions, it has been suggested that combining it with other measures such as contact tracing and monitoring can be more effective.
The Zambian study suggests that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases appear to be more prevalent in Africa at present.

Visual and screening assessments for the prevention of cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in Namibia.
In Namibia, an estimated 851,340 women are at risk of cervical cancer caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.
Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy have been confirmed to be highly effective.
However, information related to cervical cancer screening programs is lacking.
This study evaluated visual and cytology screening for the prevention of cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) in Namibia.
Findings indicate that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at a higher risk of being VIA positive.
Especially, older women with HIV have a high risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
The VIA procedure seems to work well for screening, but in the Namibian context, colposcopy should be improved and used in conjunction with positive HR-HPV results for patient management.
They recommend methods that include HPV screening for different age groups and at-risk populations (e.g., HIV positive, autoimmune disease).

The screening process can be improved by using a deep learning model that leverages previous research findings, to better address women's health goals, contemporary knowledge, and practices that align with the country's cultural context.
Women in Namibia at risk of cervical cancer need timely screening and treatment.
Many studies indicate that women are at risk of cervical cancer, however, regular screenings conducted in Namibia do not always reflect the utilization of these tests.
Researchers recommend conducting regular screenings to detect early signs, which can potentially save women from contracting the deadly disease.
Cervical cancer (cancer of the lower part of the uterus) affects the lives of many women around the world.
One major cause of cervical cancer is the human papillomavirus or HPV.
HPV is a virus that affects cervical cells and over time can cause lesions known as precancerous lesions that may develop into cancer.
Although there is a vaccine available to prevent HPV, many women in Africa, including those in Namibia, are unable to access it.
This means that it is crucial to test for the presence of the virus or lesions, especially since it is the best way to prevent cancer in these women.
According to the researchers of this study, accurate guidelines and information are needed for these hospitals to know which best practices to use.
Additionally, healthcare workers have stated that they need more information to understand how factors such as age and health influence women's risk of contracting HPV and cancer.
Common types of screening methods, known as HPV and lesions, have been studied to determine how effective they are in detecting them.
Additionally, there was an interest in testing screening methods; for example, instead of searching for lesions, examining damage by collecting cells from the cervix.
Additionally, they wanted to know if factors such as age and the presence of other diseases like HIV among women could alter their risk of contracting HPV or cancer.
Knowing this information can help hospitals and clinics to use diagnostic methods more effectively.
Researchers reviewed the records of 214 female patients who were diagnosed and treated for HPV, lesions, and cervical cancer at Windhoek Namibia Hospital.
In particular, they focused on cervical cancer, which can be easily and effectively treated at an early stage.
Information about each woman's age and overall health status was also collected.

By evaluating these records, it has been found that various diagnostic methods provide different information to healthcare professionals; similarly, they can be more beneficial before or after HPV progresses to cancer.
For example, it is often detected by collecting and examining cervical cells.
However, lesions are most often detected through visual inspection alone by employing a method called "Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid" (VIA).
The purpose of this technique is to enable doctors to obtain lesions affordably and quickly.
The reason for this is that it uses common instruments for women's uterine examinations, such as the speculum (a metal tool used to view inside the body), which is still in use today.
Most of the time, using different methods, especially in repeated examinations, has been found to provide doctors with additional information about the risk of women developing cancer.
Moreover, researchers have found that older women, especially those with HIV, have a significantly higher risk of developing cancer.
Researchers have stated that although they could obtain additional data, very few women were screened for HPV (before seeking lesions).
This could be an essential way to detect the disease very quickly.

Overall, their findings emphasize the need for Namibia's health care system to adopt affordable and effective screening methods for HPV and cervical cancer prevention strategies, in order to detect the disease in a timely manner and plan with greater caution.
The study was conducted in collaboration with scientists from Namibia and South Africa.

On a global scale, based on selected targets to eliminate hepatitis B virus (HBV), we aimed to understand the impact of treatment and improve clinical care by distinguishing individuals infected with HBV alone from those co-infected with HBV/HIV.
Experts on hepatitis B infection (HBV) from the real-world extensive cohort study under 115 have reported observational data taken from the University of Cape Town Hospital in South Africa.
HIV co-infection was found in 39 (34%) of the individuals.
A comprehensive population-based study has recorded clinical and laboratory data.

Individuals with only HBV infection, when compared to those with HIV co-infection, have a lower likelihood of being HBeAg-positive (p=0.01), being assessed by elastography (p<0.0001), and being on anti-HIV treatment (p<0.0001). Conversely, they have a higher likelihood of having detectable HBV viremia (p=0.04) and moderate/severe liver disease features, including thrombocytopenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and a high APRI score (p=0.02).
All three hepatocellular carcinoma mutations have been associated with HBV monoinfection.

Our data suggests that individuals infected only with HBV may be at a disadvantage compared to those with HIV co-infection. This highlights a potential systemic inefficiency that can occur during referral, monitoring, and treatment.
Researchers provide guidelines to improve hepatitis B treatment.
In a recent study, researchers found that co-infection with Hepatitis B (HBV) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) may help reduce HBV-only infection.
In Southern Africa, co-infection with both HBV and HIV is a serious problem.
Doctors need to understand how these viruses and the medications used to treat them work and interact with each other in order to better diagnose and treat patients.
Researchers aimed to understand the impact of treatment on patients by comparing those with only HBV to those with both HBV and HIV.
For this study, the researchers recruited 115 chronic hepatitis B (CHB) infected patients.
The samples were collected from Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Some patients who remained with HIV (39) were also infected with HBV alone.
The researchers considered race, age, and gender, and conducted numerous clinical and laboratory experiments.

Patients with only HIV have been found to have a low motivation to take antiretroviral therapy, and they also show natural signs of liver disease (this is because the HIV virus can cause severe liver disease).

Researchers have shown that individuals infected with only HBV may experience more severe damage compared to those co-infected with HIV and HBV. This is because patients infected with both viruses have a higher chance of receiving anti-HIV treatment, which also provides certain benefits in combating HBV infection.
The findings from this study will further benefit the aspects related to HIV referral, monitoring, and treatment options, which have a relative impact on co-infection with HIV and HBV.
Researchers have indicated that we should provide improved services that ensure the safety and fairness for patients who are only infected with HIV.
One limitation of this study was the small sample size used, which was restricted to one country and the hospital system within that country.
Some contemporary hospital conditions may have a contrasting perspective with this study.
In this study, further research may be necessary to accurately identify the differences found.
This paper has demonstrated a high capacity for collaboration with researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom working on this project.
Using South African patients for this study will be beneficial for a specific African population.
Additionally, this study can be used to develop better treatment plans for patients suffering from HBV, HIV, or both.
Assessment of the impact of security threats on women's employment activities in the Shiroro local government area of Niger State.

This study examines the impact of security threats on women's employment creation activities in the Shiroro local government area of Niger State, with a particular focus on women's financial independence, the type of collective employment creation activities among them, and the influence of security threats on employment creation efforts.
A survey was conducted on 377 women, and it was found that women in Shururu have high financial independence and are predominantly high job creators employed in small and medium enterprises.

The study also found that while security threats have a negative impact on women's entrepreneurial activities in the form of capital loss or disruption, the number of female entrepreneurs did not experience a significant decline.

The study suggests the creation and strengthening of community-based policy organizations to address the security challenges in the study area and the development of sustainable programs to improve women's access and benefit from financial services.
Female traders in Niger require increased security.
Researchers found that although female traders in Niger are highly industrious and financially self-sufficient, obtaining security from criminals is a challenge.

Researchers sought to understand the extent to which the safety of women leading commercial activities in the Shiroro local government area of Niger State is ensured, and how this impacts their business and financial independence.
377 women in this area were interviewed about their experiences with employment creation, financial independence, and the challenges they faced regarding their security.
Among the women, 43% reported that they were not dependent on men, while 32% reported that others were financially dependent on them.
Researchers have found that about 85% of women earn income from various commercial activities, with only a few relying solely on salary.
About 56% earn income from agriculture, and 79% earn income from trade activities.
One out of five women earn money by braiding hair, sewing, selling food, or washing clothes.
Most women (91%) reported to the researchers that they were affected by fear that their businesses might be attacked by thieves and criminals.
Due to these attacks, they lose their husbands and are sometimes forced to raise their children alone.
It has also been stated that women lack sufficient skills and capital to expand their businesses.
Researchers have reported that despite these challenges, Nigerien women have continued to perform well in their commercial activities.
It is stated that Shuroro is inhabited by people of different ethnicities and religions, and this diversity is also said to be beneficial for business activities.
This study corroborates the findings of other researchers who reported that women have lower commercial success due to their role as caregivers at home.
Instead, these researchers state that the success of businesswomen in the Niger region is largely influenced by the fear of attacks from criminals and thieves.
Researchers have suggested that all stakeholders should collaborate to address issues that pose challenges to achieving success in business.
For example, women in Niger need more financial support, access to agriculture, and security.
It is also noted that women involved in commercial activities can form groups to help combat thieves and criminals.
The maternal serum levels of selenium, copper, and zinc during pregnancy are associated with the sudden occurrence of preterm birth: a case-control study conducted in Malawi.
It means giving birth before completing the 37 weeks of pregnancy.
A study was conducted to evaluate the association of selenium, copper, and zinc levels in maternal hair with preterm birth.
In this study involving preterm birth, 181 pregnant women participated, of which 90 (49.7%) delivered on time, while 91 (50.3%) experienced preterm birth.

In general, the selenium concentration in serum, based on these baseline values, namely 47-142 ug/L, 0.76-1.59 mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, was 77.0; SD 19.4 ug/L, while the copper level was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and the zinc level was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L, respectively.
If the results are as indicated, there was no deficiency of selenium and zinc during pregnancy; a high concentration of lead was also not found in the blood.
Prenatal care was associated with iron and zinc supplementation.
Zinc, copper, and selenium levels associated with preterm birth.

Researchers have found high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc trace elements in women who experienced preterm birth. However, it is not yet known whether these high levels are derived from the foods they consume.
Preterm birth occurs when a woman gives birth before completing 37 weeks of pregnancy.
Prenatal conditions are associated with adverse health outcomes ranging from birth defects to death.
Although there can be many causes for preterm birth, the role of high micronutrient content found in food and the environment is not relatively well known.
Although these micronutrients are essential for the child's development, researchers want to understand what could happen when they are present in excess.

For this study, the researchers measured the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who experienced preterm birth, to determine how much the likelihood of preterm birth was due to these micronutrients at the time the study was conducted.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women immediately after delivery from two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital city of Malawi, between June 2016 and February 2017.

The blood samples were to be sent to a laboratory in Norway. There, the plasma (or pure blood without any mixture) was separated, and after extraction, the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc present in it were measured.
Among the 181 women included in the study, half experienced preterm birth, and among these, researchers found high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.

Additionally, they have adjusted their models to incorporate other factors such as age, overall health status, and pregnancy history, which have been identified as contributing to preterm birth beyond micronutrients.

The presence of selenium and copper in high amounts does not play a significant role in causing preterm birth, however, the presence of zinc in high amounts is associated with a sixfold increase in the risk of preterm birth.
However, the presence of the known toxic element at high levels was a concern for the researchers.
This study, which was supposed to include 600 women, was conducted on only 181 women, limiting the researchers' ability to adequately identify issues associated with high selenium levels.
No investigation was conducted on the participants' daily dietary habits to identify foods that could be sources of these three essential nutrients, and body mass index (BMI) data was not recorded.
This is the first study of its kind conducted to assess the effects of selenium, copper, and zinc on organisms found in Malawi.

Africa is one of the places with the highest rates of preterm birth. While competing with Western countries where the rate is 5%, Africa stands at 18%. Therefore, researchers want to know if nutrition plays a role in this.
The homing behavior of the pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri), site fidelity, and territoriality in Kenya.
Animals exhibit unique spatial and temporal behaviors that enhance their survival.
Understanding such behaviors is a useful measure for bringing about effective conservation and management, especially for species that are at risk of extinction.

In this study, it was found that the pancake tortoise has the ability to return home after being relocated to another place, and we also examined the species' site fidelity and territoriality within natural habitats in Kitui County, Kenya.

From July 2020 to June 2022, the behavior of 39 elephants residing in 12 distinct forested areas was monitored through radio tracking, camera trapping, and the collection of group-level dung samples and individual hair samples.
Among the aliens, fourteen radio transmitters were implanted, and their movement and behavior were monitored as they migrated from one habitat to another.

Except for two females who adapted well to the new environments they were transferred to, all other individuals attempted to return to their original habitats, with 46.15% successfully returning to their original location, while 15.38% were found within their home range, reaching areas believed to be familiar to them.
Successful replication within the lineage provides confirmation of strong spatial fidelity.

The analysis conducted on Eli's clutch size initially shows that there is no statistically significant difference among the clutches, as indicated by the number of eggs present, with an average of over 162 sample days (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P>0.05). This supports the presence of strong spatial fidelity within the population.

On the other hand, camera trapping studies and ad libitum observations have confirmed that male pancake tortoises are highly territorial, aggressively defending their territories from other incoming males.
The lost pancake bats have an astonishing ability to 'find their home'.

Researchers studying the behavior of East African pancake tortoises have made a fascinating discovery (Malacochersus tornieri): the animals are able to find their way back home after traveling long distances.
Understanding how and why they do this can be beneficial for the conservation of these endangered species.
These behaviors exhibited by the elephants are called "fission-fusion" social dynamics, and many other animals can also perform it.
The ability to return to specific locations allows animals to return to food, mates, and shelter, which enhances their chances of survival and reproduction.

Although research has been conducted on the behavior of migration in marine and freshwater eels, researchers in this study still state that what we know about migration in eels (the terrestrial phase of eels) is very limited.
In this study, the researchers aim to better understand the behavior of pangolins in their natural habitats in arid regions of Kenya.
The animals have adapted to move and feed, as well as to retreat into burrows or crevices for rest.
Researchers have observed pancake tortoise groups for about two years and have set up cameras to capture videos of the animals when they are not being directly observed.
Additionally, it observes radio emissions on 14 of the moons.
These researchers are small devices that allow tracking of animal movements and their whereabouts during day and night times.
Then, to facilitate their study, the researchers relocated some of these monitored samples to a new location.
What surprised the researchers, however, was that two of the elephants began returning to their territories from the distance of 1 to 2.5 km where they had been taken.
Researchers chose this time to relocate many animals from their habitats to observe if they exhibit similar 'return to origin' behavior.
Interestingly, about half of the elephants were able to return to the same locations they were in before their migration, often traveling more than 1.5 kilometers to reach there.
Another 15% were able to return to the general area, but they could not find the original location where they were taken from.
Researchers also know that various particles tend to settle within the same level of fluids, indicating that these particles consistently utilize the same locations for settling.
The footage of the cameras has shown that male elephants are territorial, meaning they will fend off other males attempting to enter their territory or approach their females.

Researchers have stated that the behavior of returning to the same location observed in pancake tortoises is the first of its kind, and as their findings suggest, these animals prefer to live and rest in one place as much as possible.
Their study does not explain how the eels find their way back to their habitat, so future research should focus on understanding this crucial point.
Sometimes animals need to be relocated to new environments for conservation purposes, and this information helps conservation experts ensure their safety in their new habitat.
The study was a collaboration conducted among scientists from Kenya and China, and it enhances our understanding of migratory behavior in elephants and other animals.
High-dose oral and intravenous rifampicin pharmacokinetics in patients with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia.
A trial conducted under controlled conditions.
High levels of rifampicin in the bloodstream can improve the outcomes of leprosy treatment, but it is not effective under high-stress conditions.

The exposure to rifampicin in plasma is similar between an oral dose of 35 mg/kg body weight and an intravenous dose of 20 mg/kg, as suggested by efficacy trials conducted in the context of treating leprosy.
We conducted a pharmacokinetic study on a pre-approved anti-parasitic treatment for schistosomiasis in a clinical trial with a specific cohort.
Participants with tuberculosis disease who are HIV-positive from South African hospitals were enrolled and assigned to one of the three approved rifampicin drug regimens.
Standard (oral 10 mg/kg), high dose (oral 35 mg/kg), and intravenous (20 mg/kg).
The confirmed pharmacokinetic sample was conducted on the third day.
The information was disclosed using unshared observations, and exposures were assessed using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Forty-six participants provided pharmacokinetic samples (standard dose, n = 17; high-dose oral, n = 15; intravenous, n = 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm³ (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm³).

The geometric mean area under the curve (AUC0-24) values for rifampicin from 0 to 24 hours were 42.9 mg·h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0 mg·h/ml) for the standard oral dose, 295.2 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8 mg·h/ml) for the high oral dose, and 206.5 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8 mg·h/ml) for the intravenous administration.

The rifampicin AUC0-24 GMR was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21) and the high-level drug concentration in serum (Cmax) GMR was 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23), with a high-level drug concentration of 0.89 related to oral administration under the blood vessel.
The plasma rifampicin AUC0-24 after an oral dose of 35 mg/kg was higher than that of a 20 mg/kg intravenous administration during the first few days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The findings support the use of oral rifampicin dosage in future leprosy eradication trials.
High-dose quinolones can be evaluated for HIV patients with tuberculosis meningitis.
Researchers have confirmed that starting to investigate the potential of high-dose rifampicin medication to save HIV patients with tuberculosis is beneficial.
Out of 5 HIV patients, up to 3 individuals with meningitis die due to this disease, which affects the nervous system.
Survivors sustain permanent damage to their central nervous system and the peripheral nerves that emerge from the spinal cord.
This can potentially harm their emotions and activities.
Some patients may experience falls or strokes, or have facial or limb paralysis.
A strong antibiotic medication used to prevent leprosy, rifampicin, is regularly administered in the form of a quinine to kill the bacteria that cause leprosy.
Very ill patients often struggle to fight off infections.
Additionally, rifampicin can be administered intravenously (through blood vessels) in liquid form.
The syringe is inserted into the patient's blood vessel to release the fluid into the body.
No study has been conducted so far to understand how the patient's body absorbs the medication when this method is applied.
A trained healthcare professional is required to know how to properly administer additional tools in blood treatment, hospital bed management, and the correct way to draw blood.
Therefore, it is not a viable alternative in other parts of the world where capacity is lacking.
Doctors know that rifampicin is not well absorbed in the fluid found in the eye, the ear, and the cerebrospinal fluid where the bacteria can hide.
This is why a high dosage is required to effectively eliminate all the bacteria present in the patient's body.
However, researchers were not confident about how effective and safe it could be.

Researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom wanted to determine if administering a high dose of rifampicin orally or intravenously is feasible and how each individual's body absorbs it, using a small number of patients.
Other researchers need to know this before starting large trials or tests, as they plan to administer high doses of rifampicin to many patients.
One of the three types of rifampicin treatments was administered to 46 South African patients co-infected with HIV/AIDS and tuberculosis.
The current standard treatment given to patients is quinine, and this is measured for the patient as 10 mg of rifampicin per kilogram.
The other group received a high dose of 35 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.
The third group received 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight in their blood.
Blood samples were taken from the patients after three days.
The researchers measured the amount of rifampicin present in blood plasma (the liquid component of blood).
In patients who received higher doses of quinine than those typically administered in blood treatments or regular doses, rifampicin was found in high concentrations within their bodies.
The concentration of the drug in blood plasma is similar to the high concentration and subcutaneous administration.
When patients received only the regular dose, these levels were high.
According to the researchers' explanation, this suggests that a higher dose of rifampicin could potentially improve the health of patients suffering from leprosy.
There is no problem if they are taken as pills or injected into the bloodstream - the main thing is to take them in high doses, because their body can tolerate a high level of concentration.
The results support the trial findings conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.
For example, two small trials conducted in Indonesia indicated that administering a high dose of rifampicin either orally or intravenously to many patients could potentially save lives.
As a limitation, researchers caution that the fewer participants involved than initially anticipated in this study could potentially affect the outcome.
The study was conducted in Southern Africa.
The plan supports conducting trials to test the benefit of administering high-dose rifampicin to HIV patients with tuberculosis meningitis.
This treatment is expected to save the lives of many people in Africa and other parts of the world where malaria is a major health problem.
Can the use of biochar and compost significantly improve the quality of degraded savanna soil along the coastal areas?
The reduction of soil fertility in sub-Saharan Africa is a significant barrier to crop production.
The addition of biochar and compost has been documented by many authors to have a positive impact on soil fertility.

In this study, a 30-day laboratory incubation trial was conducted using 120g samples. For this, maize cob biochar (Bebio), rice husk biochar (Rubio), coconut husk biochar (Coco300 and Coco700), or chicken manure compost (compost) and in combination with rice husk biochar (rcocomp) or in combination with maize cob biochar (cococomp) were used to amend Haplic Acrisol soil at a rate of 1% w/w.

The other treatments evaluated in the study are as follows: chicken manure compost and maize cob biochar or rice husk biochar (in order of 1% compost + 1% biochar; 1% soil w/w). This is to assess their impact on basic soil respiration, soil pH, soil microbial biomass carbon, cation exchange capacity, total organic carbon, total nitrogen, and available nitrogen content.

Since "chronic illness" and "special care" do not have a shared meaning, the aim of this study is to clarify how these concepts are applied and to provide clear definitions and appropriate interpretations.

The main characteristics of chronic diseases include a high risk of inevitable death, improper functioning of major body organs, the need for care standards to prevent death, and the ability to adapt.

The characteristics of specialized care include identifying, monitoring, and managing chronic diseases, providing support for major body systems, offering primary and continuous care, and addressing any chronic illness with specialized human and physical resources.
The definition we provided for chronic illness is "a condition where major body functions do not work properly, posing a risk of death if not treated, and the ability to recover."
The concept of special care we presented is "to identify, monitor, and support patients with chronic illnesses by prioritizing and continuously supporting the functions of major body systems."

Female genital mutilation/cutting is a traditional practice that not only violates the rights of girls but also causes numerous severe health complications.
This paper presents the reasons for female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) in three distinct countries: Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya.

Data were collected through household surveys of youth (ages 15-24) and focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, and key informant interviews conducted with youth and community stakeholders in 2016 and 2017.
Descriptive statistics and content analysis were conducted.
The findings of the study confirm the reasons previously reported in studies as causes for FGM/C, indicating that these reasons are highly interconnected and that gender norms are the main drivers.
These practices are aimed at altering the female body to conform to a "traditional" and commonly accepted patriarchal standard.
This is reminiscent of what is called 'pure body' in Indonesia, 'enhanced body' in Ethiopia, and 'intelligent body' in Kenya.
Health workers and parents play a crucial role in decision-making regarding FGM/C in all communities.
In particular, in Kenya, young women are involved in decision-making around FGM/C because their age is high when the practice is performed.

The study revealed that changes in legal and social conditions in each context lead to changes in the practice of FGM/C; this includes medicalizing FGM/C in Indonesia, delaying the age at which girls undergo the practice in Kenya, and increasing the prevalence of clandestine FGM/C procedures in Ethiopia.
The three issues indicate that the practice of FGM/C varies widely; they also highlight the different cultural meanings attributed to it by young women and their communities.
Parents have a significant influence on decision-making, with a broad interest in exploring.

The study concludes that in order for community-based strategies to bring about sustainable change, they must gain acceptance across various stakeholders due to the relationship between different FGM/C practitioners within each community.
We need to first understand why female genital mutilation occurs in order to stop it.
The practice of female genital mutilation or cutting is still carried out illegally or in secret in countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.
According to researchers, understanding why this practice occurs is key to stopping this harmful tradition and preventing the psychological and health problems it causes for women.
In certain parts of Africa and Asia, female genital mutilation (FGM), sometimes referred to as 'female circumcision', is still traditionally practiced.
Many people hold the mistaken belief that FGM is beneficial for cleanliness and to make girls modest (free from vain behaviors and humble) and to ensure that children will be obedient.
According to scientific data, FGM is not necessary for these issues.

However, in many cases, children who have undergone FGM face numerous health complications as they grow older, such as urinary infections, difficulty during urination (urinary retention), and psychological issues.
Because the practice is very harmful and violates the human rights of girls, many countries have made it illegal, yet people still perform it secretly.
In this study, researchers sought to understand why FGM occurs in different countries and what people believe about the practice.
Therefore, data on FGM was collected in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.

In each country, researchers have engaged in discussions about the practice with parents, youth, traditional leaders, health workers, and 'gerashoch' (older women who perform FGM on young girls), among other diverse individuals.

In some cases, these individuals have been personally interviewed, and they have also engaged in discussions with many people, including young intellectuals and adolescents who have suffered due to FGM.
Researchers have found that the reasons for FGM, the way it is practiced, and the beliefs surrounding it vary in each country.
Additionally, many people have been found to still be engaging in illegal activities in all the places identified.

For example, in Indonesia, people who practice traditional circumcision use a knife or blade to cut a specific part of the foreskin (a part of the body used to bring about female genital mutilation) when a child reaches 40 days old.
People believe that it is necessary to remove this 'stigma' for religious reasons as well.
In Ethiopia, FGM used to be performed early, sometimes when infants were just 7 days old.
Researchers found that people believe that one day their daughter will become a "good wife" and will be obedient to her husband and not be argumentative.
Additionally, many people believed that FGM makes childbirth easier, but on the contrary, it actually complicates childbirth.
This indicates that a girl who undergoes what is referred to as FGM is considered to have reached womanhood, and it is mostly performed when she reaches puberty.

However, in some situations, women undergo FGM even at the age of 8, and it is believed that many women are considered ready for sexual relations after FGM and are married off at a young age for pregnancy.
Researchers indicate that their findings show FGM is still practiced for various reasons.
As laws and social ideas change, how and where they are implemented also changes.
For example, parents might attempt to arrange a marriage secretly, even if it is illegal, because they may believe it is necessary for their daughter to be healthy and to find a good husband.
Understanding this is important because in some places FGM is illegal, making it difficult to conduct research on the issue, and people may not always provide truthful answers about it.

In addition to making it illegal in the future, researchers, governments, and health officials must work to correct the misconceptions about the issue and educate about the dangers it poses in order to stop FGM.

This study was conducted in collaboration with scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands as part of a large project called the 'Yes I Do Program', which aims to reduce teenage pregnancies, child marriages, and FGM.
